sections.title: Node 0 — A language that cannot do anything
sections.content:
Where this sits

This is the opening node of the whole chain. Nothing technical depends on it, but every single later node assumes you have internalised its one claim: JavaScript the language cannot do anything you can observe, and every capability you have ever used from it — printing a value, waiting, fetching, storing — was never part of the language at all. If this node doesn't fully land, every later node will feel like a grab-bag of browser trivia instead of what it actually is: one host's answer to "what should we bolt onto a language that does nothing by itself?"

Every term, from absolute zero

JavaScript — the name of the language you write. Confusingly, this is a marketing name, not the technical name of what's actually specified. There is no single canonical rulebook called "the JavaScript specification." The rulebook is called ECMAScript.

ECMAScript — the actual technical specification of the language. It is a document, formally numbered ECMA-262, published by a standards body. When people say "the JavaScript spec," they mean this document. JavaScript is an implementation of ECMAScript, the way "a Toyota Corolla" is an implementation of a set of car-safety regulations — the regulation and the physical car are different things, and several different physical cars (browsers' engines) all implement the same regulation.

Ecma International — the standards organisation that owns the ECMA-262 document. It's a Europe-based industry standards body (originally the European Computer Manufacturers Association, hence "Ecma") that also standardises other unrelated things. It is not affiliated with any single browser vendor, which matters for the history below.

TC39 — Technical Committee 39, the specific working group inside Ecma International that writes and maintains ECMA-262. When you read "TC39 proposal," it means a change working its way through this committee's process before it becomes part of the official spec. Representatives from Google, Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft, and others all sit on it and have to agree before something ships in the spec.

Specification — in this context, a precise, prose-and-pseudocode document that says exactly what a piece of software must do, without saying how to build it. ECMA-262 defines, line by line, what happens when you write 1 + "1", what a for loop must do, what a Promise must guarantee — but it never says "and then send these bytes over a wire" or "and then light up these pixels," because that's not the language's job, as this whole node exists to establish.

Engine (or JavaScript engine) — a real piece of software that reads ECMAScript-conformant source code and actually executes it: parses the text, works out what it means, and runs it. V8 (used in Chrome and Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), and JavaScriptCore (Safari) are the three that matter today. Each is written by a different team, in a different language (V8 and JavaScriptCore are C++, for instance), and each is free to implement the spec's rules however it likes internally — the spec constrains observable behaviour, not implementation technique. Two engines can differ wildly in how fast they run the same code while agreeing on every observable result, because "how fast" isn't part of what the spec governs.

Host (or host environment) — a program that embeds one of these engines and hands it extra capabilities the engine alone doesn't have. This is the central term of the whole node and gets its own section below, because understanding what it actually means — not just that it exists — is the entire point.

Host object / host-defined behaviour — the spec's own vocabulary for "a thing I am deliberately not defining, because whoever embeds me will define it." This isn't an accident of the spec being incomplete — it's a deliberate, named escape hatch built into ECMA-262 from its very first edition.

Realm — the spec's technical term for one complete, isolated "world" a piece of JavaScript code runs inside: its own global object, its own set of built-in objects like Array and Object, all fresh and separate from any other realm. You'll meet this again if you ever deal with iframes (each iframe is a separate realm, which is why an array created in one iframe fails an instanceof Array check performed in a different iframe — two different Array constructors exist, one per realm). For this node, the important fact is simpler: a host is the thing responsible for creating a realm and deciding what extra objects live in it.

Global object — the object that sits at the top of every realm, holding everything available without importing or requiring it. In a realm the ECMAScript spec builds entirely by itself, the global object would hold only spec-defined things: Object, Array, Math, JSON, Promise, and so on. Anything else that shows up on it — document, fetch, process, Deno — was put there by a host, after the engine finished setting up the spec-defined parts.

Standard library — a slight false friend worth naming, because languages like Python or Java ship one, and JavaScript's situation genuinely differs. Python's standard library (file I/O, networking, threading) ships with the Python interpreter itself, defined by the Python language project. JavaScript deliberately has no equivalent bundled with the language. What looks like a standard library in a browser (fetch, localStorage) or in Node (fs, http) is host-supplied, not language-supplied, and the two hosts' "standard libraries" share almost no API surface, because they were designed independently by different organisations for different purposes.

The history — why this exists at all

In May 1995, Brendan Eich was hired at Netscape Communications, the company that made the dominant web browser of the era, Netscape Navigator. He was given an extraordinarily tight brief: build a scripting language that could run inside the browser, and have a working version ready in about ten days, because Netscape 2.0 was already being prepared for release and marketing wanted a story about the browser being "programmable." He wrote the first working version in that window. It went through a few names before landing on the one that stuck — internally called Mocha, briefly shipped as LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript specifically to piggyback on the buzz around Sun Microsystems' unrelated Java language, which was fashionable at the time. The two languages share almost nothing beyond some surface syntax borrowed from C; the shared name was a marketing decision, not a technical relationship, and it has caused confusion for three decades since.

The problem Eich was actually solving was narrow and concrete: before this, making a web page do anything beyond display static content required a full round trip to a server. Validating that a form field wasn't empty, showing or hiding part of a page, reacting to a mouse movement — every one of these meant sending a request over the network (often over a dial-up modem, at the time) and waiting for an entire new page back. Netscape wanted a lightweight language that could run directly inside the browser and manipulate the page the user was already looking at, without that round trip. That's the shape of the very first host: Netscape Navigator 2, embedding this brand-new engine, and handing it exactly the capabilities a browser needed to be useful — reading and writing the parts of a page, popping an alert box, reacting to a click.

The language succeeded immediately and chaotically. Microsoft, needing Internet Explorer to compete, reverse-engineered Netscape's language rather than licensing it, and shipped their own implementation in Internet Explorer 3 in 1996, calling it JScript — a different name specifically to sidestep any trademark claim from Netscape/Sun over "JavaScript." JScript and Netscape's JavaScript were close, but not identical, and they diverged further with each release, since neither vendor was working from any shared written specification — only from Netscape's original implementation as the de facto reference. Web developers were left writing code littered with browser-detection branches just to work around behavioural differences between the two.

This divergence is what forced standardisation. In November 1996, Netscape submitted the language to Ecma International specifically to get an implementation-independent written specification that Microsoft, Netscape, and anyone else could be held to — a document neither company controlled unilaterally. That effort produced ECMA-262, first published in June 1997, and its language name inside the document was deliberately neutral: ECMAScript, avoiding both "JavaScript" (Netscape/Sun's trademark) and "JScript" (Microsoft's). That is the entire reason two different names exist for what is, for almost every practical purpose, the same language — one is the brand, the other is the standard the brand implements.

Here is the detail this node exists to surface: from that very first 1997 edition, the specification explicitly declined to define any I/O. It defined values, expressions, functions, objects, and how to evaluate a program written using them — but it built in an explicit concept of "host objects," things the spec says exist and behave a certain way only because whatever environment embeds the language chooses to provide them. This wasn't an oversight or something added later under pressure. It was the design, from day one, because the same language needed to be usable inside Netscape's browser, inside Microsoft's browser, and — Netscape had ambitions here too — potentially inside entirely different products with entirely different needs, like server software. A specification that hard-coded "here is how you talk to a browser's screen" would have made the language useless anywhere else. Leaving I/O undefined, and building an explicit extension point for hosts to fill in, is what let the exact same language later run inside Node.js in 2009 — a context with files and network sockets and no screen at all — without changing a single rule in ECMA-262 to make that possible.

The mechanism — traced

Concretely, here is what happens when a JavaScript engine is asked to run a program, and exactly where the boundary this node is about actually sits.

An engine is handed a string of source text — your code. The engine's first job, entirely specified by ECMA-262, is parsing: turning that text into a structured internal representation the engine can act on (in practice, most engines eventually produce bytecode, then further optimise hot code into machine code — but none of that internal detail is what the spec constrains; the spec constrains observable results, not internal representations). The engine's second job is evaluation: walking through that structure and carrying out the operations it describes, according to rules the spec writes down in extraordinary, almost pedantic detail. For example, ECMA-262 spells out, as a sequence of numbered abstract steps, exactly what happens when you write 1 + "1" — how each operand is converted, in what order, to what intermediate type, before the final concatenation happens and produces the string "11". Every quirky JavaScript coercion rule you've ever hit exists because some specific numbered algorithm in this document says so, not because an engine improvised.

Evaluation happens inside a realm, and the realm's global object is populated in two phases. First, the engine itself creates and installs everything the spec actually defines — the Object constructor, Array, Math, JSON, Promise, and every other built-in ECMA-262 specifies, plus the global functions the spec itself defines, like parseInt and encodeURIComponent. This phase is identical no matter what host is running the engine, because it's pure language, governed entirely by ECMA-262 with zero host involvement. Second — and this is the phase that actually matters for this node — the host, before or as it lets your code run, adds its own objects and functions onto that same global object. A browser's host code adds document, fetch, setTimeout, localStorage, and hundreds more. Node's host code instead adds things like process, require, and a global object carrying its own different set of capabilities, defined by an entirely separate specification process (Node's APIs are documented by the Node.js project itself, following none of TC39's process, since they were never a TC39 concern to begin with).

This is directly demonstrable, and worth actually trying rather than taking on faith. Most JavaScript engines can be embedded with essentially no host code attached at all — this is exactly what a "sandboxed" or "isolated" JavaScript environment is, and small embeddable engines built for exactly this purpose exist (QuickJS is a commonly cited one). Run a program in an environment like that, and typeof console comes back "undefined", typeof setTimeout comes back "undefined", and there is no way to make the program produce any output an outside observer could see — its return value can only be read by whatever embedded it, because nothing about "showing something to a person" was ever the language's job. Meanwhile typeof Array, typeof JSON, and typeof Promise all still come back correctly, because those genuinely are language-level, defined by ECMA-262 itself, requiring no host cooperation whatsoever.

Put the two phases together and the whole node compresses into one operational fact: the global object in any running JavaScript program is language-defined built-ins plus whatever a specific host chose to bolt on, and every capability you've ever associated with "JavaScript" that isn't in the first category came from the second. console.log, despite being the very first thing almost anyone types when learning the language, is entirely host-supplied — both the browser and Node happen to provide something called console with a method called log, but they are two unrelated implementations that happen to share a name and a rough shape, maintained by entirely different projects, and a hypothetical third host is under no obligation to provide either.

What an interviewer does with this

"Is JavaScript single-threaded?" is a very common opener, and a strong answer starts exactly here rather than jumping straight to the event loop: the language specification doesn't mention threads at all — it's silent on concurrency entirely — so "single-threaded" is a property of specific hosts' typical configuration (a browser's page, or a default Node process), not a property of the language itself. Node can run multiple threads via its worker_threads module, and a browser page can run genuinely parallel code via Web Workers; both are true precisely because threading was left to hosts to decide, exactly like I/O was.

"What's the difference between JavaScript and ECMAScript?" is asked almost verbatim, and the strong answer is the standards-history one above, in miniature: ECMAScript is the specification (ECMA-262, maintained by TC39 at Ecma International); JavaScript is the common name for engines that implement it, and the two names exist specifically because of the Netscape/Microsoft trademark situation in the mid-1990s, not because they refer to different things technically.

"Why doesn't window exist in Node.js?" is a weaker-sounding but genuinely diagnostic question — a weak answer says "because Node is different"; a strong answer says window was never part of the language to begin with, it's the name the browser host happens to give its global object, and Node's host code populates the same underlying global-object mechanism with an entirely different set of names (global, process) because it's solving a different problem with no concept of a window at all.

"What makes code 'isomorphic' or 'universal' — able to run in both the browser and Node?" is the practical payoff of this whole node: code is portable exactly to the extent that it only touches things ECMA-262 itself defines (arithmetic, Array methods, Promise, plain objects) and avoids anything either host bolted on. The moment code touches document or fs, it has silently taken a dependency on one specific host's extension of the language, and it will throw a reference error the instant it's run somewhere that host's objects don't exist.
